title: Contains Duplicate
kidExplanation: You have a big toy box. You pick up toys one by one. For each toy, you ask: 'Have I already seen this exact toy before?' If yes, you shout 'Duplicate!' If you finish the whole box with no matches, every toy is unique.
plainProblem: You are given a list of numbers. Return true if any number appears at least twice. Return false if every number is unique.

thinkingSteps.title: Brute force idea
thinkingSteps.body: Compare every number with every other number. It works, but if the list has n items you do about n×n checks. That gets slow fast.

thinkingSteps.title: Why it is slow
thinkingSteps.body: Looking at pairs means the work grows like a square. Interviewers want better than that when they can.

thinkingSteps.title: Aha insight
thinkingSteps.body: What if we keep a notebook of numbers we already saw? Checking the notebook must be quick — that notebook is a hash set.

thinkingSteps.title: Better idea
thinkingSteps.body: Walk the list once. If the number is already in the set, return true. If not, add it. One pass, fast lookups.

pattern.name: Hash set / hash map for seen items
pattern.whenToSpot: You need fast lookups of values you already saw.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def containsDuplicate(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        # Notebook of numbers we have already seen (hash set)
        hashset = set()

        # Look at each number in the list, one by one
        for n in nums:
            # Have we seen this number before?
            if n in hashset:
                # Yes — found a duplicate
                return True
            # No — remember it for later
            hashset.add(n)
        # Finished the list with no duplicates
        return False

complexity.timeReason: We look at every item once, so time grows with the list length.
complexity.spaceReason: In the worst case the set remembers every unique number.

edgeCases: All same values → true on the second item.
Negatives and zeros are normal numbers too.
commonMistakes: Sorting first without saying the extra time cost (sorting is O(n log n)).
Using a list for 'seen' instead of a set — lookups become slow.
Forgetting to add the number after you check it.
interviewTips: Say out loud: 'I need O(1) average lookups, so I will use a hash set.'
Mention the trade-off: extra memory for speed.
Offer the sorting alternative if the interviewer asks about less memory.
interviewApproachNotes: Hash-set one-pass is the standard Google-friendly answer: simple code, O(n) time, clear trade-off vs sorting. Prefer this over nested loops. Sorting is acceptable as a follow-up if they constrain memory.
